At the temple fair in their kasba, Hari could not stop talking about Ira's singing.

"Did you hear her? That voice! She should be on the radio."

Swati smiled and said, "Yes, lovely." Ira taught with Hari at the government school, and she had sung a bhajan on the small stage while half the town went quiet.

Walking home past the closed shops, Swati felt something heavy settle in her chest. She could not sing. She taught tailoring to girls in the back room of her mother's house. Nobody went quiet when she spoke.

"You're quiet," Hari said.

"Just tired."

She wasn't angry at Ira. Ira had done nothing. It was more that Hari's praise had held up a mirror, and Swati had looked into it and found herself smaller. She didn't like the feeling, and she didn't know what to do with it.

qa.a: On the small stage at the temple fair.

qa.a: She feels small and jealous, measuring herself against Ira and finding herself short, though she isn't angry at Ira.

qa.q: What could Swati try with this feeling?
qa.a: She could notice that it is a comparison rather than a real threat, and maybe tell Hari honestly that she felt small, without blaming Ira.

qa.q: How does Hari see his praise of Ira?
qa.a: To him it is simple admiration for a good singer; he likely doesn't realise it made Swati feel small.

grounding: Swati hears her partner praise a colleague's singing and feels small, showing jealousy as a hidden comparison in which she finds herself short.

Ivan came back from the architecture firm's party in Istanbul glowing. "You should see Elena's designs. She's brilliant. Honestly, the best in the office."

Zeynep, who was still a student, said, "That's great," and kept stirring the soup.

She had met Elena once: tall, relaxed, fluent in three languages. Ivan had laughed at all her jokes.

It wasn't even about Ivan. Not really. She realised she was jealous of Elena for being everything Zeynep thought she wasn't yet.

She came out of the shower and said nothing. But she felt it all evening, like a stone in her shoe.

In the college research lab in Chennai, Ankur leaned over Rashmi's bench. "This is beautiful work, Rashmi. Really clean data."

Jaya, at the next bench, kept pipetting. Ankur was her boyfriend. He'd never said "beautiful" about her data.

At lunch in the canteen he mentioned Rashmi twice more: her poster, her question at the seminar. Jaya pushed rice around her plate.

That afternoon, her own experiment failed again. She looked at her messy notebook and thought of Rashmi's neat charts, and felt her throat tighten.

It isn't Ankur, she told herself. He isn't doing anything wrong. It's that I'm measuring myself against her and coming up short.

Knowing that didn't make the feeling go away. But it helped a little to know its real name.

"You'd probably rather be travelling with Neha from your office," she said, laughing, as if it were a joke.

Parveen had started making little jokes. "Oh, you're texting Sana again? Should I leave you two alone?" Kamal laughed the first few times. By the second month he didn't.

In their shared Mumbai flat, she tested him in other ways. She'd go quiet for a whole evening to see if he would notice and chase. He noticed. He asked. She said, "Nothing." He stopped asking after a while.

One night, while he showered, she read his chats with Sana, his colleague. Presentations. Deadlines. One joke about their boss. Nothing else.

She felt a rush of relief. Then, an hour later, the fear crept back: maybe they deleted things.

Kamal came out of the bathroom and saw his phone on her side of the bed. He didn't say anything. But he looked at her in a way he never had before, tired and a little distant.

The thing she feared most was starting to happen, and she had helped it along.

"Can I tell you something about me? Not about you."

Sachin looked over. "Okay."

"When you go out with your college friends and don't message for hours, I feel insecure. My mind makes up stories. I know that's mine to work on. It's not something you're doing wrong."

"I'd like a bit of reassurance sometimes. Like a message saying you're having fun. But I'm not going to ask to see your phone or demand proof. I don't want to be that person."

Sachin was quiet for a moment. Then he shifted the bags to one hand and took hers with the other. "Thank you for telling me like that. I can send a message. That's easy."

Neelam felt her shoulders drop for the first time in weeks.

Wednesday

Today I saw Neelam crying outside the office with her mummy. I heard the principal say "sorry about your grandfather" and "take as many days as you need."

Nobody else saw. Only me!

In class everyone was asking where Neelam went. I almost told them. I had the words right in my mouth. It felt like holding a hot samosa, like I would burst if I didn't tell.

I didn't tell them. Yet.

But I kept thinking how Riddhi and Mahi would look at me if I knew something they didn't. Like I was important.

Now I am in bed and I feel a bit funny about it. Neelam was crying. Maybe it's not a nice thing to tell.

— Maria

Shalini was sent to fetch chalk from the headmaster's room at the village school near Hassan. At the door she stopped.

Gauri from her class was inside, crying, while her father spoke quietly with the headmaster. Shalini heard "the loan" and "the land" and "we may have to leave."

She ran back with the chalk, her heart pounding. She knew something! Something nobody else knew!

At the water tap during break, her classmate Karthik was filling his bottle. Shalini tugged his sleeve. "Guess what I know about Gauri."

Karthik looked up, curious. "What?"

Shalini opened her mouth. Then she remembered Gauri's red eyes, the way her shoulders shook.

"Tell me!" Karthik said.

Shalini hesitated, the secret still warm and exciting in her chest, and not sure anymore whether it was hers to give.

qa.q: What was Shalini sent to fetch?
qa.a: Chalk from the headmaster's room.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling as she ran back with the chalk?
qa.a: She was excited and felt important, her heart pounding because she knew something nobody else did.

qa.q: What could Shalini do at the water tap?
qa.a: Tell Karthik it isn't hers to share, because Gauri was upset and the news is Gauri's family's private business.

qa.q: How might Gauri feel if the class found out?
qa.a: She would probably feel ashamed and hurt, on top of worrying about leaving.

grounding: Shalini overhears a fragment about a crying classmate's family and feels important and eager to tell, hesitating on the edge of sharing it.

Monday. Urmila saw Deepa's mother arrive at school in the middle of maths and take Deepa home early. Deepa was crying.

Tuesday. On the walk home, Urmila told her best friend Saurabh. "Deepa's mother took her home crying." Saurabh didn't look very interested, so she added, "I think her parents are getting divorced. Her mother looked really angry."

She hadn't seen an angry face. She had only seen Deepa crying. But saying it made the story better, and Saurabh's eyes went wide.

Thursday. Urmila told the story again to her cousin. This time she said, "Her parents are getting divorced," without the "I think." It sounded true now. She almost believed she'd seen the angry face herself.

Friday. Deepa came back to school. Her grandmother had been in hospital. That was all.

qa.q: Why had Deepa actually gone home early?
qa.a: Her grandmother had been in hospital.

qa.q: Why did Urmila add the detail about the divorce?
qa.a: Saurabh didn't look very interested, and she wanted the story to be more exciting; she enjoyed his eyes going wide.

qa.q: What could Urmila have done differently?
qa.a: Say only what she saw, Deepa leaving crying, or not share it at all, instead of adding a guess.

qa.q: How might Deepa feel if she heard the divorce story?
qa.a: She would probably feel hurt and confused, since it wasn't true and she was already worried about her grandmother.

grounding: Over a week Urmila retells what she saw to her best friend, adding a guessed detail that sounds truer each time she tells it.

Thomas, a story about your friend got bigger as it went round, you said? Let your Pema aunty tell you what I did as a girl in Darjeeling.

One morning our neighbour's daughter, Dolkar, came to school with a bandage on her hand. That was all I saw.

I told my best friend, Nima. A bandage wasn't exciting, so I said, "I think she got into a fight with the milkman's boy." Nima gasped, and I loved it.

A week later, the story was that Dolkar fought boys daily and had been sent away from her old school. Even I started to believe it.

Then Dolkar's mother came to our house, very upset. Dolkar had cut her hand on a tin while cooking.

The turning point, Thomas, was that little "I think." There I chose excitement over truth.

qa.q: How had Dolkar actually hurt her hand?
qa.a: She cut her hand on a tin while cooking.

qa.q: Why did young Pema add the detail about Dolkar's brother?
qa.a: She wanted the story to be exciting and enjoyed Nima's gasp.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Pema's story?
qa.a: The moment she added "I think she got into a fight with the milkman's boy," choosing excitement over the truth.

qa.q: How did Dolkar's mother feel when she came to the house?
qa.a: She was very upset, probably hurt and angry that a false story about her family had spread.

grounding: Pema aunty recalls adding a guessed detail to what she saw when telling her best friend, and how the guess grew and sounded truer with each retelling.

It was raining so hard that the whole school was kept indoors for lunch. Sangeeta and Pallavi sat in a corner of the hall.

"Guess what," Sangeeta whispered. "I saw Megha's father come to school today. He was talking to Ma'am for a long time."

Pallavi shrugged. "So?"

Sangeeta wanted her to be excited. So she added, "He looked really angry. Megha must have done something bad. Maybe she stole something."

She had not seen an angry face. The father had looked tired, if anything.

Pallavi's eyes widened. "Stole? What?"

"I don't know. Something big, probably."

By the end of lunch, Sangeeta had half convinced herself it was true. It sounded so real when she said it.

After the bell, Megha walked past, head down. Sangeeta suddenly didn't feel excited at all.

qa.q: Why was the whole school kept indoors for lunch?
qa.a: It was raining so hard.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta feel when Megha walks past after the bell?
qa.a: She no longer feels excited; she feels uneasy and guilty about the story she made bigger.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do now?
qa.a: Tell Pallavi that she made up the stealing part, so the guess doesn't keep spreading as if it were true.

qa.q: What might Megha be feeling as she walks past with her head down?
qa.a: She may be sad or worried about whatever brought her father to school, unaware of the rumour.

grounding: On a rainy indoor lunch, Sangeeta tells her best friend what she saw and adds a guess to make it exciting, half believing it herself.

Monday. Mehak watched the whisper start at the back bench. Sonal leaned to Tina: "Don't tell anyone, but Rinku's father lost his job." Tina's eyes went round.

Tuesday. At lunch the whisper had reached the girls by the window. Mehak heard it again, with an extra part: "and they're selling their car." Each person said, "Promise you won't tell," and then told.

Wednesday. Jatin, who usually sat alone, leaned over to Mehak's group. "Did you hear about Rinku? They're selling their house too." The group turned to him, surprised, and let him sit with them for the first time.

Mehak saw his face light up. He wasn't saying it to be mean, she thought. He was saying it so they'd let him in.

Rinku, two rows ahead, was colouring her map, not knowing.

qa.q: What extra part had been added by Tuesday?
qa.a: "And they're selling their car."

qa.q: What does Mehak think about why Jatin joined in?
qa.a: She feels uneasy but understanding, believing he repeated it not to be mean but to be let into the group.

qa.q: What could Mehak do to stop the chain?
qa.a: She could refuse to pass it on and quietly tell her group it's Rinku's private matter, or tell a teacher if it keeps spreading.

qa.q: How might Rinku feel if she knew what was being whispered?
qa.a: She would probably feel embarrassed and hurt, especially since some parts, like the house, may not even be true.

grounding: Mehak watches a rumour travel in "don't tell anyone" whispers, and sees Jatin repeat it to feel part of the group.

passage:
Kavitha, you don't know whether to join the whispering about the new girl? Let your Jagdish dadu tell you what I saw in my village school.

A boy named Bhola came to our class from the city. Someone said his mother had run away. Nobody knew if it was true. But everyone whispered, "Don't tell anyone," and then told everyone.

I watched my friend Mohan, who was always left out of games. One day he whispered it too, louder than anyone. The big boys laughed and let him play kabaddi with them that evening.

I understood then. Mohan didn't care about Bhola's mother. He wanted to belong.

The turning point, Kavitha, came when our teacher heard it and sat us all down. Bhola's mother was working in Delhi. I've never forgotten Bhola's face that week.

qa.q: Where was Bhola's mother actually?
qa.a: Working in Delhi.

qa.q: What did young Jagdish realise about why Mohan repeated the rumour?
qa.a: He realised, with some sadness, that Mohan didn't care about the story; he felt left out and wanted to belong.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: When the teacher heard the rumour and sat the class down, showing the truth about Bhola's mother.

qa.q: How do you think Bhola felt that week?
qa.a: He was probably hurt, lonely and ashamed, as the new boy whispered about by everyone.

grounding: Jagdish dadu recalls watching a rumour spread with "don't tell anyone" and seeing a left-out boy repeat it to belong.

The bus was stuck in traffic for forty minutes after school, so the whispering had plenty of time to travel.

Himani, in the window seat, watched it go from the back row forward. "Don't tell anyone, but Sweety's brother got caught cheating in his exam." Each child leaned to the next. "Promise you won't tell." Then they told.

When it reached Jeevan, the quiet boy in the seat across the aisle, Himani expected him to shrug. Instead he turned to the boys in front and said, "I heard he's getting thrown out of college, even." They turned around, interested. One of them offered Jeevan a chip.

Jeevan grinned. It was the first time anyone on the bus had shared with him.

Himani looked at Sweety, sitting near the front with her headphones in, and felt her stomach twist.

qa.q: How long was the bus stuck in traffic?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when she looked at Sweety?
qa.a: Her stomach twisted; she felt uneasy and sorry for Sweety, who didn't know what was being said.

qa.q: What small step could Himani take?
qa.a: She could refuse to pass it on and, if it keeps spreading, tell a teacher, since it is about Sweety's family.

qa.q: Why might Jeevan have joined in so eagerly?
qa.a: He was usually left out, and repeating the rumour, even adding to it, made the other boys include him.

grounding: On a stuck bus Himani watches a rumour travel with "promise you won't tell", and sees a left-out boy repeat it to belong.

I noticed it on Tuesday. Girls stopped talking when I came into the washroom. Two of them giggled behind their hands at assembly.

At lunch my friend Naveen told me, looking at his shoes. "They're saying your father is in jail."

My face went so hot I thought it would melt. My father isn't in jail. He's working on a ship and he comes back in three months. But he once went to the police station to report our stolen cycle. Someone must have seen.

I wanted to hide in the library forever. Then I wanted to hit someone. I didn't know which.

I went home and told Amma everything, crying. She held me and said, "You haven't done anything wrong." The next morning she came with me to see my class teacher, who spoke to the class that same day.

— Sangeeta

qa.a: She listened, comforted Sangeeta, said it wasn't Sangeeta's fault, and went along to the class teacher, who spoke to the class that day.

qa.a: He was probably uncomfortable and sorry, looking at his shoes, but wanted Sangeeta to know.

grounding: Sangeeta notices stares and giggles, learns a partly false rumour about her father, and feels shame and anger before turning to her mother and teacher.

Teacher's note, Class 5B, Thursday

In drawing, several children kept glancing at Pooja and giggling. Pooja kept her head down and pressed so hard with her crayon that it snapped.

At break she stayed at her desk. When I sat beside her, she said, very quietly, "They're saying I wet the bed at the class picnic. I didn't. I spilled my water bottle."

Her face was red, and her fists were tight. "I want to hit Rohini. Or never come back."

I told her it was not her fault and that I was glad she told me. I stayed with her through break. Then I spoke to the class, without naming anyone, about how stories get twisted and how they hurt.

I phoned Pooja's mother after school and will watch Rohini's group tomorrow.

— Joseph Sir

qa.a: Pooja spilled her water bottle.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel when she told Joseph Sir?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and angry, wanting to hit Rohini or never come back, and confused because the story was twisted from something real.

qa.q: What did Joseph Sir do that helped?
qa.a: He stayed with Pooja, said it wasn't her fault, spoke to the class about twisted stories, and phoned her mother the same day.

qa.q: How might Rohini's group feel after the class talk?
qa.a: They may feel a little embarrassed or guilty, realising the story wasn't true and was hurting Pooja.

Friday

Worst day ever.

Everyone was looking at me and giggling. At lunch Meenu told me: they're saying I copied my science project from the internet.

I did NOT. My Nani helped me cut the pictures, that's all, and I wrote everything myself. But I did look at one website for the volcano picture. So it's half true and half a lie and I don't even know how to explain it.
